one_liner: JVM microservice framework (Netty-based) whose gRPC server out-served the stock gRPC C++ async server at 2-4 CPUs in one grpc_bench run.
what_it_does: Armeria is a Java/Kotlin server and client framework from LINE, built on Netty, that serves gRPC, Thrift, REST, gRPC-Web and Protobuf-JSON from one port and one Server object. A gRPC service is the ordinary grpc-java generated ImplBase class registered through GrpcService.builder().addService(...) on Server.builder(); existing grpc-java service code moves over with only the bootstrap changed. It is not a C++ library: the catalog entry exists because a Java service on it beat a C++ gRPC server in an independent benchmark.
how_it_is_fast: Armeria's GrpcService runs its own gRPC framing on Armeria's Netty HTTP/2 stack (the grpc module depends on grpc-core, grpc-stub and grpc-protobuf but not grpc-netty), and, unlike upstream grpc-java, it runs service logic directly on the event-loop thread rather than handing each call to a separate executor (documented under 'Blocking service implementation'). No source attributes the grpc_bench margin over C++ to a mechanism. In run #559 Armeria's CPU per request stayed at 17.9-23.6 us from 1 to 4 CPUs while the C++ server's rose from 18.0 to 47.4 us (derived from page data), so the gap comes from the C++ server not scaling on that build, not from Armeria being cheaper per request.
when_to_use: JVM shops that already run grpc-java and want one server for gRPC, gRPC-Web, Protobuf-JSON, Thrift and REST on a single port, with throughput at or slightly above plain grpc-java (run #559: 0.98-1.06x the grpc-java G1GC row).
Small unary RPCs with non-blocking handlers on 2-4 cores, where the event-loop-inline execution avoids a thread hop.
Teams that need an off-the-shelf gRPC server with gRPC-Web for browsers, unframed JSON access and server reflection, without an Envoy sidecar for gRPC-Web translation.
Services where heap memory of hundreds of MiB is acceptable and JIT warm-up can be absorbed before traffic.
when_not_to_use: Memory-constrained deployments: run #559 shows 570-679 MiB average for Armeria against 21-32 MiB for the C++ server (about 20-28x).

Tail-latency-sensitive single-core services: at 1 CPU Armeria matched the C++ throughput but its p90 was 58.18 ms against 19.93 ms and p99 65.14 ms against 21.81 ms; at 2 CPUs its p99 was still worse (46.85 vs 39.43 ms) despite 1.28x the throughput.

Handlers that block (JDBC, file I/O, synchronous HTTP): service code runs on the event loop by default, so blocking stalls every connection on that loop unless @Blocking or useBlockingTaskExecutor(true) is used.

Large or complex request messages: issue #5152 (open since 2023-08) reports p95 rising from about 100 ms on raw grpc-java to about 300 ms on Armeria for ~500 KB requests at 10-12K QPS, traced to deserialization on the I/O thread.
When the fastest JVM gRPC server is the goal: in the same run Vert.x gRPC served 1.78x Armeria's req/s at 1 CPU and Pekko gRPC 1.29x.

integration.dependencies: Netty, grpc-java core/stub/protobuf/services, protobuf-java (HEAD pins Netty 4.2.18.Final, grpc-java 1.84.0, protobuf 3.25.9); grpc-kotlin optional
integration.min_toolchain: Java 8 or later for users (README); the benchmark image used Temurin JDK 23
integration.platforms: any platform with a supported JVM
integration.thread_safety: Service methods run on Netty event-loop threads by default; blocking work must be moved to ServiceRequestContext.blockingTaskExecutor(), the @Blocking annotation or GrpcServiceBuilder.useBlockingTaskExecutor(true) (docs).
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial — not a replacement for the C++ gRPC library; for grpc-java service implementations it reuses the generated ImplBase stubs, so only the server bootstrap changes

gotchas: The C++ baseline collapses with core count rather than Armeria pulling ahead: cpp_grpc_mt went from 57,403 req/s at 1 CPU to only 85,485 at 4 CPUs (1.49x) while its CPU per request rose from 18.0 to 47.4 us (derived from page data); at 1 CPU, where both burn one core, the two servers tie. The C++ server pre-posts a single CallData per completion queue on the legacy async API and links the unpinned Debian libgrpc++ of the gcc:15.2.0 image, so the 1.28-1.65x margin measures that build and pattern on this host, not C++ codegen.

Armeria is not special among the JVM rows of the same run: the plain grpc-java 1.58 Netty server (java_hotspot_grpc_g1gc, same JVM flags minus the Armeria header switches) was 1.7% ahead at 1 CPU and 1.0% ahead at 2 CPUs, and Armeria led it by about 6% at 3-4 CPUs; any JVM gRPC server here beats cpp_grpc_mt at 2+ CPUs.

At 3-4 CPUs the top rows (Vert.x 149-153k, Pekko 141-142k, Quarkus 140-142k req/s) cluster with idle server CPU (Vert.x 225-230%, Pekko 261-271%), and Armeria used 330.65% of 400% at 4 CPUs, which points to the 11-CPU ghz client capping the run near 150k req/s; the 4-CPU ratio is client-bound and not a server ceiling.

The benchmark server is tuned (Date and Server headers off, -Dcom.linecorp.armeria.validateHeaders=false, PROTO-only serialization, 70% heap) and pins armeria 1.20.3 (2022) with grpc-java 1.58.0, still the pins at grpc_bench HEAD, while Armeria is at 1.42.0 (2026-10-06).
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick Armeria over Vert.x gRPC or Pekko gRPC when you want grpc-java's own service API plus gRPC-Web, JSON transcoding and Thrift on one server; pick Vert.x gRPC or Pekko gRPC when raw unary throughput per core matters, since both beat Armeria at every CPU count in run #559, and tonic or grpc-go when memory footprint matters.
verified_claims_summary: In grpc_bench run #559 (maintainer, commit c4c93b3, 2026-04-23, Xeon Gold 6548N, server Docker-capped at 1-4 CPUs and 4 GiB, ghz 0.114.0 client on 11 CPUs, 50 connections and 1000 concurrent complex_proto unary echoes, 120 s after a 30 s warm-up, one run per setting), Armeria 1.20.3 on Temurin 23 with G1GC served 0.98x, 1.28x, 1.65x and 1.64x the req/s of cpp_grpc_mt (g++ 15.2.0 -O3 -flto glue over Debian-packaged libgrpc++) at 1, 2, 3 and 4 CPUs. Three other published runs (#441, #475, #547) have Armeria at 0.03-1.02x of the same C++ server, so the win is specific to this run's C++ build and host.
status_note: Actively developed by LINE (release 1.42.0 on 2026-10-06, 5,257 commits, 5.1k stars, 621 open issues), Apache-2.0 and copyable as Maven artifacts; the benchmarked 1.20.3 build is about four years and 22 minor releases old.
